# Local patches carried on the vendored three.js 0.186.1 build

This directory is GENERATED by `node tools/gen/vendor-three.mjs 0.186.1` from the
pristine npm tarball (`three-0.186.1.tgz`, sha256 in `MANIFEST.json`): the readable
`build/three.{webgpu,core,tsl}.js` are patched by the exact-count edits in
`vendor/three-patches/patches.mjs`, then minified with the pinned `terser`
(package.json devDependency; `@rollup/plugin-terser` at default options is what
upstream produced its own `.min.js` files with through r185). `MANIFEST.json`
records the tarball, the terser version, the patch ids and a sha256 per file;
`node tools/gen/vendor-three.mjs --check` verifies the files against it with no
network, and `tests/unit/gfx-backend-canary.test.mjs` pins each patch's surviving
shape in the minified output (property names and string literals — never terser's
local names, which change between runs of the tool).

Why a generator: three.js removed its minified builds in r186 (PR #33893, "jsDelivr
minifies on its own"). The unminified WebGPU bundle is 444 KB gzipped against 195 KB
minified, and every earlier patch recipe here was a `sed` against mangled names in
upstream's min file. Patching the readable source is both the only option left and
the more robust one.

Never hand-edit the `.min.js` files: `--check` fails, and the next regeneration
discards the edit. Change `patches.mjs` and re-run the tool; update this file by hand
(it is the rationale, not generated).

## Bumping to a new release

1. `node tools/gen/vendor-three.mjs <version>` (needs npm through the proxy; or
   `--tarball` a file you fetched). A patch whose needle finds the wrong number of
   sites STOPS the tool — upstream changed the shape; read the new source before
   re-deriving the edit, and check the "upstream" note on each patch below for the
   release that retires it.
2. `grep -rn "three-0\.<old>"` outside `docs/notes` — the import map in `index.html`,
   `sw.js`'s optional precache, `js/game.js`'s `preloadThreeVendor()`, the spike
   harness, `docs/archive/moves/spike-backends.json`, the tests and docs all name the
   directory. `git rm -r` the old directory.
3. `node --test tests/unit/gfx-backend-canary.test.mjs`, `npm run test:service-worker`,
   `npm run test:tooling-fast`, then the render-tlx rule gate (`gfx-probe` on Lavapipe
   WebGPU, plain + `tlxForceHw=env` + `shadow`), `tests/specs/tlx-probes.spec.js`, and
   a `gpu-census.yml` leg on `macos-latest` — a software probe is not evidence about a
   player's GPU.

Patch ids keep their historical numbers so the comments that cite them
(`tsl-lit.js` "§4", `tlx.js`) stay true.

## 1. swizzle — Chromium 141 rejects the r185+ texture-view descriptor

`src/renderers/webgpu/descriptors/GPUTextureViewDescriptor.js` sets `this.swizzle =
'rgba'` in the constructor AND `reset()`, passed unconditionally into every
`createView()`. Chromium 141 validates `swizzle` as a `GPUTextureComponentSwizzle`
dictionary, so the string throws on every render pass: shadow alloc dead, env probe
dead, `present()` throws on the first race frame → TLX refuses the tab and reloads.
Identity swizzle carries no information, so the member becomes `undefined`
(`this.swizzle=void 0` after terser; the canary counts both sites).

Still unfixed upstream as of r186 and on `dev` (2026-09-22): no feature gate
(`device.features.has('texture-component-swizzle')`) anywhere under
`src/renderers/webgpu/`; the member's doc comment now says "requires the feature;
ignored otherwise", which is not what Chromium 141 does. Chrome ships the feature
as a DevTrial from 142. The correct upstream fix is that gate. No issue is filed;
the draft is `docs/notes/UPSTREAM-THREE-ISSUES.md` §1 — put its URL here once posted.

## 2. #33952 bind-group leak — RETIRED in r186 (PR #33954)

`Bindings._destroyBindings()` now removes the destroyed bind group from the shared
texture's `bindGroups` Set upstream. The canary asserts the upstream form
(`bindGroups.delete(`) is present so a re-drop of an older release fails. The deferred
material `dispose()` in `js/render/three/tlx.js` and `tsl-fx.js` stays as it is — it
is correct against the fixed upstream too.

## 3. #34405 polygonOffset missing from the WebGPU pipeline key — RETIRED in r186 (PR #34406)

`WebGPUBackend.getRenderCacheKey()` / `needsRenderUpdate()` carry `polygonOffset`,
`polygonOffsetFactor` and `polygonOffsetUnits` upstream, so TLX's bias-only material
variants (the `tsl-fx.js` road decals, `tsl-lit.js`'s `o.depthBias`) no longer share
one `GPURenderPipeline`. The canary asserts the key includes the three fields.

## 4. WebKit's 8 KB private address space — render-stage node variables move into main()

iOS/Safari 26 refuses any WGSL module whose module-scope `var<private>` declarations
sum past 8,192 bytes:

```
Render pipeline creation failed (renderPipeline_MeshBasicNodeMaterial_41):
The combined byte size of all variables in the private address space exceeds 8192 bytes
```

`WGSLNodeBuilder` emits every node variable (`.toVar()`, property nodes, inlined `Fn`
temporaries) as a module-scope `var<private>`; Apex's lit fragment declared ~1,600 of
them (~12.4 KB), so the owner's iPhone drew the sky and nothing else (2026-09-03), with
zero GPU errors reported until the `uncapturederror` listener form landed. Dawn does
not check the sum, so no software or Metal Chromium run ever saw it.

The builder has the function-scope form already — `getVars( stage, false )` emits
`var name : type;` with a tab indent, and the COMPUTE template places it inside
`main()` when `allowGlobalVariables` is false — but the render templates never did.
Three edits: `buildCode()` passes `shaderStage === 'compute' && allowGlobal` to
`getVars`, and the vertex and fragment templates move their `// vars` block from
module scope to the top of `main()`.

Safe for every shader this game generates: no helper `fn` (three's `tsl_*` layouted
functions) reads a node variable — only `main` does (`artifacts/wgsl-dump-iphone`,
checked 2026-09-03). A TSL graph that reads a `.toVar()` from inside a `setLayout`
function would break under this patch; none of ours does, and
`js/render/three/tsl-chunks.js` keeps the layouted noise helpers pure. `varyings`,
`output` and `instanceIndex` stay `var<private>` (a few dozen bytes). Still unfixed on
`dev` (2026-09-22; the related TSL perf issue #34386 / PR #34531 does not touch the
scoping). No issue is filed; the draft is `docs/notes/UPSTREAM-THREE-ISSUES.md` §2.

## 5. Warm-up yields tasks instead of display frames without scheduler.yield

`Renderer.compileAsync()` awaits `yieldToMain()` after every projected render object,
cached pipelines included. The upstream fallback (`src/utils.js`) is
`requestAnimationFrame`: without native `scheduler.yield` that is one display-frame
wait per object while Apex deliberately holds the game loop during compilation, and
hidden tabs stop it entirely. Native `self.scheduler.yield()` is kept unchanged,
receiver included; only the fallback becomes a `MessageChannel` task (both ports closed
before resolving), with `setTimeout(resolve, 0)` where `MessageChannel` is absent.
Never a resolved Promise/microtask, which does not yield to input or rendering.

The canary exercises the actual vendored function body: native method preservation,
asynchronous/concurrent completion, both-port cleanup, absence of animation-frame
waits, and the timer fallback. Unchanged upstream as of r186 and on `dev`
(2026-09-22). No issue is filed; the draft is `docs/notes/UPSTREAM-THREE-ISSUES.md` §3.

## 6. #34535 `getDynamicCacheKey` allocates an array PER RENDER OBJECT PER FRAME

`hash$1` is `( ...params ) => cyrb53( params )`, so every call mints a rest array, and
`RenderObject.getDynamicCacheKey()` calls it up to three times. `get needsUpdate()`
calls `getDynamicCacheKey()` for every render object on every draw, so the arrays are
(objects × frames) of pure garbage. Measured on the three.js/WebGPU path before the
patch: 255 KB/frame of JS allocation, 28.4 MB/s, a collection about once a second
freeing a median 25.8 MB (`tools/gfx/frame-hitch.mjs`).

The fix is upstream's: one module-scope scratch array, filled by index and hashed with
`hashArray` (already in the bundle). The key VALUE changes — a flat hash of five slots
replaces three nested hashes — which is safe because this method is the key's only
producer and every consumer compares its output to itself. First carried by #228;
re-landed alone after its revert (the revert's black screen came from the skip-draw
patches 7 and 8, which stay out — PERF-FINDINGS §2af).

Upstream: PR #34553 (issue #34535), milestone r187 — RETIRE THIS ON THE r187 BUMP.

## 9. `TextureNode.update` rebuilds an unread UV matrix for every sampled texture on every draw

`TextureNode.update()` runs per render OBJECT whenever the node carries a matrix OR a
flipY uniform, and it called `texture.updateMatrix()` (`Matrix3.setUvTransform`: a cos, a
sin, nine writes) whenever `texture.matrixAutoUpdate` is true, even when the node has
no matrix uniform, so nothing reads the result. Three's WebGL2 backend gives every
texture node a flipY uniform, so every shadow-map compare, material-array and lamp-bake
sample paid it on every draw: census 289 (real Metal, montreal night) sampled 293 ms of
`setUvTransform` self time in a 21.9 s WebGL2 leg. The patch rebuilds the matrix only
when this node has a matrix uniform. Any node that samples through the matrix still
refreshes it, so texture offset/repeat/rotation behave exactly as before.

Ids 7 and 8 stay unused: they were #228's skip-draw patches, reverted (PERF-FINDINGS §2af).

Upstream: unfixed on dev as of r186.

## 10. TextureNode: one shared flipY / uv-matrix uniform per BASE node (backport of #34552)

Every TextureNode minted its OWN flipY uniform (three's WebGL2 backend always flips)
and matrix uniform, and marked itself OBJECT-update to feed them, so each `.sample()`
clone added one more entry to the per-object update set and the object UBO. Apex's
lit shader samples ~27 texture nodes per draw, 20 of them PCF taps on four shadow
maps: ~33 per-object updates per lit draw on WebGL2 (census 289: `updateForRender` +
`update` + `updateReference` ≈ 28 % of the leg's CPU).

Upstream's r187 fix moves both uniforms onto the base node as `onObjectUpdate`
uniforms. This backports that shape: the uniforms live on `getBase()` and read the
base's CURRENT `value` on each object update (a node whose `.value` is swapped still
reports the new texture), and the node itself is `NodeUpdateType.NONE`. `sample()`
also carries the base's `updateMatrix` to the clone, so a base marked
`setUpdateMatrix(false)` yields clones without the uv matrix. The lit shader
(`tsl-lit.js` `shadowMapNode`) samples each shadow map through one such base.
Patch 9's edit is left in place but is dead code once this applies (the old
`update()` is no longer called).

Upstream: PR #34552 ("TextureNode: Simplify and optimize uniforms"), r187 — RETIRE
THIS AND PATCH 9 ON THE r187 BUMP.

## 11. WebGL MRT MSAA resolve blits the depth buffer once per colour attachment

`WebGLBackend._resolveRenderTarget` builds one `blitFramebuffer` mask
(`COLOR | DEPTH [| STENCIL]`) and reuses it inside the per-attachment MRT loop, so
TLX's two-attachment scene target (`output` + `ssrTag`, `tlx-post.js`) resolved its
MSAA depth into the same depth texture twice a frame on desktop WebGL2 (HIGH 2x,
ULTRA 4x). The second resolve writes identical bytes: on ANGLE-D3D11, which cannot
`ResolveSubresource` depth, it is a whole extra full-screen shader pass. The patch
clears the depth/stencil bits after the first blit (`mask&=~(…DEPTH_BUFFER_BIT|
…STENCIL_BUFFER_BIT)` survives terser). A single-attachment target runs the loop once,
so nothing else changes.

Upstream: unfixed on dev as of r186.

## 12. Uniform-array buffers re-upload on every render even when unchanged

A `NodeUniformBuffer` (every `uniformArray`) inherits `Buffer.update() === true`, so
each render-group version bump (every `renderer.render`) re-uploads it in full
(`bufferData` on WebGL2, `queue.writeBuffer` on WebGPU). Apex's lit frame block
(4 × 48 lamp rows + `matTexScale`, ~3.3 KB in five bindings, `tsl-lit.js`) went up once
per builder state per render, ~70 states × 2 passes, unchanged all day
(TLX-PERF-HUNT 2026-10-11 §A2).

`Bindings` now asks `_uniformBufferChanged(backend, binding)` before
`backend.updateBinding` at both call sites. It compares the CPU bytes (a `Uint32Array`
view, bitwise, so `-0` and NaN payloads count as changes) with a copy of the last bytes
sent to THAT binding's GPU buffer and skips an identical upload. The copy lives in the
backend's data record for the binding (`uboSrc` / `uboWords` / `uboLast`), so:
- it dies with the GPU buffer (`destroyUniformBuffer` deletes the record), and a fresh
  buffer always uploads first;
- one uniform node feeding several programs has one record per program's buffer;
- a `setup()` that swaps the typed array (a resized array) rebuilds the view and uploads;
- WebGL's `updateBindings` (a full re-upload on bind-group creation or a texture swap)
  clears it;
- update ranges, non-node uniform buffers and anything that is not a 4-byte typed array
  bypass it (the old always-upload path).

Upstream: unfixed on dev as of r186.

## 13. Texture bindings in a SHARED uniform group (renderGroup)

Every sampled texture sits in three's per-object group, so every render object of every
pass walks each of its texture bindings in `Bindings._update` (`binding.update()`, a
`textures.get`, a `backend.get`, a `cacheKey` string). Apex's lit shader carries ~8-11
of them. In a shared group (`renderGroup`) `NodeManager.updateGroup` lets the first
object of each `renderer.render()` do that walk and the rest skip it (perf hunt 3
R2/B14; `bench-tex`: 0.7-1.6 µs per object at K = 10). Two things stopped a texture
joining a shared group:

- **(a) the cache key.** `NodeBuilder._getBindGroup` keys a shared group on
  `binding.nodeUniform.id`, which `NodeSampledTexture` / `NodeSampler` do not have — a
  TypeError on the first build. A texture or sampler binding is now named by its
  texture node's id **and its binding name**: the group's binding objects are the FIRST
  builder's, three's WebGL backend sets each program's sampler units by NAME
  (`_setupBindings`: `getUniformLocation(program, binding.name)`), and one texture node
  gets a different `nodeUniformN` name in different programs of one fragment graph (the
  attribute-instanced and InstancedMesh lit programs: `nodeUniform28` vs `nodeUniform32`).
  Keyed by id alone, the second program would have taken the first one's names and
  sampled the wrong units. Ids also get separators now (`12`+`3` was `1`+`23`).
- **(b) `TextureNode.clone()`** builds a fresh node, so every `.sample()`, `.compare()`,
  `.load()` and `texture(node, …)` tap of a grouped base fell back to `objectGroup`. The
  clone keeps its source's `groupNode` (TextureNode's own `clone()` only; the
  `ReflectorNode` / `PassTextureNode` overrides are untouched).

Nothing in three sets a group on a texture node, so both edits are inert until a caller
opts a texture in: `tsl-lit.js` does for its shadow maps, lamp bake, material arrays,
lamp grid and env cube under `SHARED_UNIFORMS`, with `apex26.tlxSharedTex=0` as the A/B.
Safe because every TLX `.value` swap of those textures (`setEnvCube` around a probe face,
`setMaterialMaps`, `updateFrame`'s `setLampBake`) happens between `render()` calls, and
`updateGroup` re-runs the walk once per call.

Upstream: unfixed on dev as of 2026-10-13 — the key moved to
`Bindings.getSharedBindGroup` with the same `binding.nodeUniform.id`, and
`TextureNode.clone()` still drops `groupNode`
(https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/src/renderers/common/Bindings.js,
https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/src/nodes/accessors/TextureNode.js).

## 14. Rejected pipeline error scopes and diagnostics stay within the owning pipeline

The synchronous render/compute paths called `popErrorScope().then(success)` without
handling rejection. The asynchronous paths used an async Promise executor: their
`finally` resolved the outer compilation promise while a rejected await escaped
through the executor's ignored return value. Both leaked `OperationError: Instance
dropped in popErrorScope` independently of TLX's synchronous render catches.

All four paths now handle scope rejection, mark the affected pipeline `error`, and
report a reason capped at 300 characters. Sync paths await shader diagnostics in
the same handled chain; async paths use an async function directly with a catch,
so compilation promises settle after either failure. Existing validation and WGSL
source diagnostics remain intact; failure to read compilation info is handled too.
This does not suppress window errors, alter shaders, or classify rejection as a
device loss. The existing device-loss recovery remains responsible for real loss.

The canary executes the actual generated `WebGPUBackend.pipelineUtils` methods
with GPUDevice mocks in both modes: rejected scopes, rejected diagnostics, ordinary
validation, rejected asynchronous pipeline creation, and successful compilation.
It checks no unhandled rejection, pipeline failure markers, balanced scopes,
bounded logging, preserved shader excerpts, and settled compilation promises.

Present in pristine three 0.186.1. API references checked 2026-10-15:
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/GPUDevice/popErrorScope
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/Promise

## 15. The WebGL fallback frees GL programs, shaders and VAOs (three #34597, issue #2651)

iPhones run TLX on three's WebGL backend. In 0.186.1 `Pipelines._releaseProgram`
only calls the stats-only `info.destroyProgram`, `WebGLBackend` never deletes a
program, shader or VAO, and `vaoCache` keys on a growing attribute id, so every
track switch leaves its VAOs, programs and shaders behind while the buffers are
freed. `tools/gfx/gl-object-census.mjs` (WebGL2 prototype create/delete counters,
picker mode, monza → monaco → spa × 3 on SwiftShader) measured, before the patch:
VertexArray / Program / Shader deleted = 0 at every step, live +149 / +12 / +24
per three-circuit cycle (about +50 / +4 / +8 per visit). Numbers after the patch:
`docs/notes/GL-OBJECT-LEAK-2026-10-17.md`.

What it does (backport of upstream #34601 and a reduced #34610):
- `Backend` gains no-op `destroyPipeline` and `deleteVertexState`; `Pipelines` calls
  `backend.destroyPipeline` on release and `backend.destroyProgram` beside
  `info.destroyProgram`.
- `WebGLBackend.destroyProgram` deletes the GL shader, `destroyPipeline` the GL program.
- VAOs keep their attribute-id key (the stable id #34610 also relies on), plus a
  reference count (`vaoUsed`). A render object acquires one reference the first time it
  draws and releases it in `RenderObjects.onDispose` or before its geometry-dispose
  handler drops `attributes`; the VAO is deleted when the last holder lets go (and the
  state cache's bound VAO is reset first). Compute VAOs are pinned (count never drops).
  The full #34610 re-keys and moves the logic into `WebGLVertexArrayUtils`; that part is
  not needed for the leak and is not carried.
- The WebGPU backend inherits the no-ops; `destroyProgram` now also runs there and only
  drops its data-map entry.

Upstream: fixed on dev for r187 (not published; npm latest is 0.186.1). Retire this
patch at the r187 bump. References: https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/issues/34597,
https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/pull/34601, https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/pull/34610
